name: Prize crossword No 22,165
preamble: Five down clues are undefined and their location has to be sorted out.

clue.text: Conceal first a little stream, then a greater

blocks.note: a piddle is a small trickle, and the Piddle is also a small Dorset river
the Trent is one of England's major rivers, a greater stream
to conceal is to hide

explanation.surface: Instructions for hiding something: first in a small brook, then in a bigger river.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, this down clue has no definition: PIDDLETRENTHIDE is a Dorset village. 'Conceal' is written first, but 'first ... then' puts the two streams ahead of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says five down answers are villages left undefined, and Piddletrenthide is a real village in the Piddle valley of Dorset.

clue.text: Colourless, devoid of fashion

blocks.note: white can be thought of as the absence of colour
devoid of something is lacking it
ton is an old word for high fashion or the fashionable set

explanation.surface: A dull, drab outfit with no style at all.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition here, as the preamble warns. TON for fashion comes from French 'bon ton', the stylish world of Regency society.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves this down entry undefined; Whitelackington is a small English village in the West Country near Ilminster.

clue.text: End organic modification of male attributes

indicators.note: a modification changes something, so the letters are altered into a fresh order

blocks.note: the two words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: A call to stop genetically altering the traits of males.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End' looks like a verb meaning stop; it simply lends its letters to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Androgenic describes what produces or relates to masculine characteristics, as androgen hormones such as testosterone do.

clue.text: Archbishop Fisher's quarry

blocks.note: Stephen Langton was Archbishop of Canterbury at the time of Magna Carta
a fisherman hunts fish such as the herring

explanation.surface: What did Geoffrey Fisher, Archbishop of Canterbury, go hunting for?
explanation.walkthrough: Geoffrey Fisher really was an Archbishop of Canterbury, so the surface reads as one man; split apart, the archbishop is a different one and the fisher is an angler.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by design as the preamble says; Langton Herring is a real village on the Dorset coast beside the Fleet lagoon.

clue.text: Most yeast strains can produce undesirable swelling

indicators.note: to strain is to sieve out, so a few letters are filtered from the words in front

blocks.note: the letters straddle the join between these two words

explanation.surface: A warning that most yeast cultures can cause unwanted swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strains' reads as varieties of yeast, but it is the instruction to filter letters out of 'Most yeast'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed, painful bump on the eyelid, a small infected lump nobody wants.

clue.text: Season arrived without being carried

blocks.note: winter is one of the four seasons
borne is the past participle of bear, to carry
arrived means came

explanation.surface: The season turned up on its own feet rather than being brought.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition, as the preamble warns. The pieces are not used in clue order: the carrying part sits between the season and the arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the five undefined down entries; Winterborne Came is a small Dorset parish near Dorchester, where the poet William Barnes was rector.

clue.text: Tanner, the name of youth leader

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a tanner was old British slang for a sixpence coin
a handle is informal for a name
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Tanner is the surname of the person who heads the youth group.
explanation.walkthrough: Tanner looks like a surname or a leather worker, but it is pre-decimal British slang for a sixpence, a small silver coin. This entry is undefined per the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves it undefined; Sixpenny Handley is a real village in north-east Dorset on Cranborne Chase.

clue.text: Strange habit in unknown part of Asia Minor once

indicators.note: something strange is out of the ordinary, so the letters fall into an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written
x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: An odd custom found in some obscure corner of ancient Anatolia.
explanation.walkthrough: The unknown letter joins the other seven before they are all mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bithynia was an ancient kingdom and later Roman province in north-west Anatolia, the region now in modern Turkey.

clue.text: £1 accepted by idiot - not so bright

indicators.note: whatever is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a twit is a fool
L is the abbreviation for pound (libra), and 1 looks like the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A fool who gratefully pockets a single pound is not very clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so bright' looks like a jibe at the idiot's intelligence, but it is the definition, meaning dim light. The pound sign gives L from Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: Twilit means lit only by twilight, the dim glow after sunset, so the scene is less than fully illuminated.

clue.text: One's oversight may make the front page

definitions.text: One's oversight may make the front page

blocks.note: surface reading: someone's careless slip or blunder that turns into headline news
setter's reading: oversight as supervision, the person who decides what goes on page one

explanation.walkthrough: Oversight usually means a mistake, suggesting an embarrassing scandal; here it means supervision, the job of the person running a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's chief journalist supervises its content and chooses which stories lead on page one.

clue.text: King Kong, perhaps, about to eat fruit

indicators.note: about can mean around, so one piece is placed surrounding another

blocks.note: a grape is a fruit
taken as written

explanation.surface: The giant movie gorilla is just on the point of munching some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as one phrase meaning 'on the verge of'; split it, and 'about' wraps the fruit around the eating.
explanation.definitionFit: King Kong is a giant gorilla, and gorillas belong to the great apes along with chimpanzees and orangutans; 'perhaps' marks an example.

clue.text: Trade in wood and port

blocks.note: first meaning: to do business, buy and sell
second meaning: pine or fir timber in planks
third meaning: a coastal town in Kent, on England's south-east coast

explanation.surface: A merchant does business in timber and in fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' tempts as the drink, a natural pairing with trade; here it is a harbour town. Three meanings, not the usual two.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for doing business, a noun for softwood planking, and the name of a Kentish seaside town.

clue.text: Result of earthquake to which property may be subject?

definitions.text: to which property may be subject

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: the earth torn open

blocks.clueFragment: to which property may be subject
blocks.note: second meaning: the annual charge a leaseholder pays the landowner

explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally the answer is a split in the earth; as an idiom it is a fee. In Britain leasehold flats and houses often owe the freeholder this yearly sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally soil torn apart by a quake, and in property law the regular payment owed by a leaseholder for the land.

clue.text: Term of office?

blocks.note: surface reading: a period of tenure in a political or official post
setter's reading: the stretch of the day spent at a desk in a workplace

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase suggests a mayor's or president's tenure; the question mark warns that the office is an ordinary workplace and the term a working day.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names standard working hours, nine in the morning until five in the afternoon, the typical desk-job day.

clue.text: Copy of leading track sport

indicators.note: what leads goes at the front, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: its opening letter
racing is a sport

explanation.surface: A replay of the race leader in a track event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading track' sounds like a front-runner on the circuit, but it takes just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracing is a reproduction made by drawing over an original through thin transparent paper.

clue.text: Strange man? Blair is held to be quite the opposite

indicators.note: something strange is odd and out of place, so the letters are rearranged
being held means being gripped inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: taken as written
Tony Blair, UK Prime Minister when this puzzle appeared

explanation.surface: Is Blair an odd fellow? People think he's the reverse of that.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname gives the first name: TONY sits inside the rearranged man.
explanation.definitionFit: An antonym is a word with the contrary meaning, so it is literally the opposite of another word.

clue.text: See 4
Record in entire chaos - that's careless

indicators.note: chaos is total disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement
in places one piece inside, enclosed by the other

blocks.note: a disc is a gramophone record
taken as written

explanation.surface: Leaving your record collection in total disarray is sloppy.
explanation.walkthrough: The mixed letters are split around the record, with two before it and four after.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiscreet means lacking prudence about what one says or does, a thoughtless kind of heedlessness.

clue.text: Elegant stock

blocks.note: first meaning: tidy, smart and well proportioned
second meaning: an old word for cattle, bovine livestock

explanation.walkthrough: 'Elegant stock' suggests fine shares or goods; 'stock' here is livestock, the sense surviving in neat's-foot oil.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for trim and stylish, and an archaic noun for oxen or cows kept on a farm.

clue.text: As eggs with hair would be, comparatively speaking

definitions.text: As eggs with hair would be, comparatively speaking

indicators.note: what the letters would be once changed, a hint that they become something else

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Picture hairy eggs: they would be more tousled than ordinary ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay at once: eggs given hair would be hairier, and those two words supply the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaggier is the comparative of shaggy, meaning more covered in long rough hair, as hairy eggs would be beside smooth ones.

clue.text: Letter to volunteers from No 10

indicators.note: to here means attached onto, so one piece is joined to the end of another

blocks.note: the figures 1 and 0 look like the letters I and O
the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: Downing Street writes to thank volunteers.
explanation.walkthrough: No 10 Downing Street is the Prime Minister's office, but the number is read as the two letters it resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth character of the Greek alphabet, equivalent to the Roman I.

clue.text: Sport with a subversive appearance

blocks.note: the FA, the Football Association, governs English football
Jack Cade led a rebellion against Henry VI in 1450

explanation.surface: A sport that looks as though it is undermining the established order.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking 'Sport' as a body that runs a sport is loose but common; 'a subversive' is one named rebel, so the 'a' adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A facade is a deceptive outward show, a false front concealing what lies behind it.

clue.text: Nifty as a Dior fashion model

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or mould, so the letters are formed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the Model T was Ford's famous early motor car

explanation.surface: A catwalk model wearing Christian Dior looks very smart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion model' reads as one phrase about the catwalk; split, 'fashion' rearranges the letters before it and 'model' is the car.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit means skilful and dexterous, and nifty is an informal synonym for being deft or clever.

clue.text: There's no end to war decoration at the right time of year

blocks.note: taken as written
VE Day, Victory in Europe, marked the end of the Second World War in Europe
the MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Wars go on forever, and medals are handed out right on schedule each year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There's no end to war' sounds like a cynical lament; it is three pieces. The month is apt: Remembrance and Armistice Day fall in it.
explanation.definitionFit: November is the eleventh month, a period of the calendar, and the season when the Armistice is commemorated.
